newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: ARGENTINE FARMERS SEEN SOWING RECORD COTTON CROP.
newsitem.headline: ARGENTINE FARMERS SEEN SOWING RECORD COTTON CROP.

text.p: Good prices for cotton and the need to utilize the growing infrastructure from recent investments have Argentine farmers planning to sow a record 1.2 million hectares with 1997/98 cotton, despite a disappointing 1996/97 crop, a top exporter said.

"The sowing intention for the coming season is very good. Even though the costs are high and the problems associated with cotton always rife, the price, at about $500 for raw cotton, is very good," Rafael Almiroty, of Almiroty y Cia, told Reuters.
He added that producers have made big investments in cotton machinery in recent years and also that cotton is by far the most attractive crop available to farmers in northern Argentina.
The manager of the Argentine Cotton Chamber, Matilde Vetti, agreed that the industry was optimistic about sowing.
"Some are talking about an increase of 20 percent in area, others of 40 percent," she said, adding that the chamber was preparing its own forecast.

"People are talking about 1.2 million hectares," Almiroty said. "If we have a reasonable spring followed by a fairly good January and February, then Argentina could easily produce more than 450,000 tonnes of lint, whch would be a new record."
Farmers have now almost completely finished harvesting the troublesome 1996/97 crop. The harvest was marred first by storms, which forced much resowing, and then by drought and heat.
Final production came to around 315,000 tonnes of lint, produced from 980,000 tonnes of raw cotton, Almiroty estimated.
The area sown with cotton was about 956,000 hectares in 1996/97, down slightly from a record one million hectares the previous season.
"Production turned out to be a bit better than feared," he said.

He said that about half of the crop was good quality, but that the other half, harvested in areas hit by excess rain, suffered from an assortment of defects including impurity and dirtiness as well as problems with length and resistance.
Almiroty described the average ginning yield of 32 percent as a good result given the unfavorable weather and ascribed it to genetic improvements in cotton varieties.

Most of the crop has already been sold, with around 190,000 tonnes of lint assigned to export buyers, mainly in Brazil and then other near neighbors such as Chile, and about 80,000 tonnes going to the local textile manufacturers.
Lower than expected production and rising prices led to an unusual number of cancellations and renegotiations of sales contracts, Almiroty said.
"The people who bought at low prices were basically those who didn't get their cotton, or had to renegotiate," he said.
A bad Paraguayan cotton crop, battered by weather and boll weevils, also encouraged some sales and some smuggling of Argentine cotton to feed Paraguay ginners, he said.
Boll weevils -- the bane of cotton farmers -- have been detected recently in Argentina, but Almiroty said that the problem seemed under control.
